title: Mandarin From a Person, Not a Screen
text:
Very young babies can tell apart the speech sounds of almost any language. By around their first birthday, they have become specialists, getting better at the sounds of their own language and worse at foreign ones. Patricia Kuhl and her colleagues at the University of Washington asked whether a short burst of exposure to a foreign language could keep that ability alive, and what kind of exposure would work.

They brought nine-month-old American babies from English-speaking homes into the lab for twelve short sessions over about four weeks. In each session, a native Mandarin speaker read books and played with toys while talking to the baby. A comparison group had the same kind of sessions in English.

Afterward, the babies were tested on a pair of Mandarin sounds that English does not distinguish. Infants who had played with the Mandarin speakers could tell the sounds apart about as well as babies of the same age growing up in Taiwan. The English group could not.

Then came the key test. Other American babies watched the same Mandarin speakers, saying the same things, on a video screen, or heard only the audio. These babies learned nothing measurable. The social presence of a real person seemed to be what made learning happen.
lesson: Small children learn language from people, not screens. Talking, reading and playing face to face does what no recording can.
people: Patricia Kuhl, Feng-Ming Tsao, Huei-Mei Liu
source: Kuhl, P. K., Tsao, F.-M., and Liu, H.-M. (2003). Foreign-language experience in infancy: Effects of short-term exposure and social interaction on phonetic learning. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 100(15), 9096-9101.
